title: Your Company Is Becoming a Software Factory, Even Outside Engineering
author: Dr. Hernani Costa
summary_short: Companies are becoming distributed software factories as non-engineering teams create AI workflows across operations, finance, procurement, and compliance. OpenAI and Anthropic are building enterprise agents for cross-functional work. The management challenge shifts from tool selection to workflow ownership, review standards, and control architecture. McKinsey data shows high performers redesign workflows rather than just expanding access.
summary_medium: The AI transformation is no longer confined to engineering departments. OpenAI's Frontier platform and Anthropic's Claude Code are explicitly designed for enterprise agents that operate across business processes, systems of record, and team workflows. McKinsey's 2025 survey reveals that AI high performers are nearly three times more likely to have fundamentally redesigned workflows, distinguishing them from organizations that simply expand access. This pattern signals that the next software factory will be distributed across the business rather than housed in one department. Non-engineering teams are already producing machine-executable work: support teams building triage agents, procurement creating intake and approval flows, finance developing forecasting pipelines, compliance generating evidence packs. The central management question evolves from tool selection to workflow ownership, review standards, permissions, and escalation paths. The scarce resource becomes review capacity, not prompt writing. Eurostat data shows 32.7% of EU adults used generative AI in 2025, with 63.8% among 16-24-year-olds, indicating the next workforce expects AI-native environments. The 90-day action plan involves mapping existing informal work, selecting three to five meaningful workflows outside engineering, defining review thresholds, assigning ownership by layer, and creating scorecards for cycle time, correction rate, and cost per accepted result.
summary_long: The enterprise AI landscape is undergoing a fundamental shift that extends far beyond traditional engineering boundaries. OpenAI's Frontier platform and Anthropic's Claude Code are explicitly architected for enterprise deployment, enabling AI agents to operate across business processes, systems of record, and team workflows rather than serving as isolated chat assistants. OpenAI frames this explicitly as production infrastructure for AI coworkers and business processes spanning customer support, procurement, revenue operations, financial forecasting, and software engineering. Anthropic's Claude Code supports specialized subagents for task-specific workflows with improved context management, while computer-use tooling enables autonomous multi-step interaction with software environments through screenshots, keyboard, and mouse control. McKinsey's 2025 State of AI survey provides quantitative validation: AI high performers are nearly three times more likely than others to have fundamentally redesigned individual workflows, and they are scaling agents across more business functions than peers. This workflow redesign is identified as one of the strongest contributors to meaningful business impact. The organizational implications are profound. Support teams can design triage and escalation agents rather than merely answering tickets. Procurement can run guided intake, document comparison, and approval preparation flows instead of processing vendor requests. Finance can create reviewable forecasting and reporting pipelines beyond building spreadsheets. Compliance can generate evidence packs, retrieval-assisted controls, and exception workflows rather than just writing policy documents. The critical insight is that review capacity becomes the scarce resource as machine-generated work spreads across the business. Organizations must decide which workflows are permitted, what systems agents can access, which outputs require human approval, how exceptions escalate, and how quality is monitored over time. This represents a fundamental shift from prompt libraries to review and control architecture. Eurostat data reveals that 32.7% of people aged 16 to 74 in the EU used generative AI tools in 2025, including 15.1% for work purposes, with usage reaching 63.8% among 16 to 24-year-olds. This dual signal indicates AI is entering companies through everyday work rather than formal procurement channels, and the next generation of employees will expect AI-native environments by default. The organizational design requires distributed ownership: executive teams own the overall AI operating model including risk tiers and value measurement, technology teams own platforms and security controls, business functions own workflow design and outcome quality, and risk and compliance own policy and boundaries. Without this distribution, companies face either centralized bottlenecks or unmanaged sprawl. The recommended approach separates workflows into three categories: assistive workflows that support employees without acting independently, managed workflows that complete process parts with review checkpoints, and autonomous workflows operating under strong controls. Most companies should begin in the first two categories, focusing on controlled compounding rather than maximal automation. The 90-day action plan for European leaders involves mapping departments already creating machine-executable work informally, selecting three to five repetitive and reviewable workflows outside engineering, defining review thresholds before scaling, assigning ownership by layer, and creating scorecards tracking cycle time, correction rate, approval rate, and cost per accepted result.
